messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 42

# Marcus

Marcus sits with his hands folded in his lap, his wedding ring catching the light as he shifts slightly in his chair. At sixty-one, he carries himself with the careful posture of someone who has learned to move through the world deliberately. For thirty-two years, he has worked in nonprofit administration, most recently overseeing community development programs in his city. His colleagues describe him as steady, reliable—the kind of person who remembers everyone's names and asks about their families.

Three years ago, on an ordinary Tuesday morning, Marcus was driving to work on the interstate when a delivery truck swerved into his lane without warning. He remembers the sound first—a terrible screech of tires and the metallic shriek of impact. His sedan was crushed between the truck and a concrete barrier. He recalls the sensation of being trapped, the smell of burning rubber and fluid, the taste of blood in his mouth. A passerby called 911. He spent two weeks in the hospital with a fractured ribs, a punctured lung, and lacerations across his left side. Physically, he healed. The doctors said he was fortunate.

But something fractured inside him that day that the doctors could not see on an X-ray.

Now, Marcus avoids the interstate entirely. His commute to the nonprofit office, which once took twenty minutes, now takes fifty—he navigates surface streets with white-knuckled intensity, his eyes constantly scanning the road. His wife, Priya, notices that he grips the steering wheel so tightly his knuckles turn pale. When she offers to drive, he becomes irritable, insisting he is fine, though his jaw remains clenched the entire journey.

At night, Marcus lies awake beside Priya, his body drenched in sweat, his heart racing from nightmares he cannot quite remember upon waking. He dreams of the collision repeatedly—sometimes he is trapped in the car as it fills with water; other times he watches helplessly as Priya is the one crushed by the truck. He has stopped going to bed at the same time as his wife because his thrashing disturbs her sleep. Instead, he sits in the living room after midnight, scrolling through his phone or watching television with the volume low, waiting for exhaustion to overtake him.

His work has suffered in ways he cannot fully explain to his supervisor. He used to attend community meetings, visit partner organizations, engage directly with the people his nonprofit served. Now he finds reasons to stay in the office—delegating fieldwork to younger staff members, citing administrative tasks that suddenly seem urgent. The irony is not lost on him; he has dedicated his career to serving others, yet he increasingly cannot manage the simple act of driving across the city to meet them.

When he does venture out, Marcus is hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. Every car that approaches from behind triggers a spike of panic. He finds himself bracing for impact, his muscles tensing involuntarily. He has nearly caused accidents himself because he flinches unexpectedly at sudden movements in his peripheral vision. Once, a car door slammed in a parking lot and Marcus found himself on the ground, gasping, unsure how he had gotten there.

Priya expresses concern gently but persistently. She notices he has stopped attending their weekly dinners with friends, that he declines invitations, that he seems withdrawn even when present. He is short-tempered in ways uncharacteristic of him—snapping at her over minor frustrations, then feeling immediate remorse. He knows something is wrong. He knows the accident was three years ago and he should be over it by now. But the fear remains vivid, immediate, and inescapable.
